Claude Code has fundamentally changed how I work. But somewhere around week three of using it for anything non-trivial, I started noticing the same friction points appearing over and over.

The first one is review. Complex workflows produce artefacts — plans, drafts, designs, structured outputs. Reviewing them inside a running conversation is awkward. You end up scrolling, copy-pasting, losing your place. What you actually want is a proper review interface: see the thing, decide what you think, feed that decision back into the session cleanly.

The second is launching. Once you've built a few workflows, you have a collection of them. But remembering the exact invocation — the slash command, the arguments, the right context — becomes its own cognitive tax. You spend mental energy on the meta-work of starting work instead of the work itself.

The third is parallelism. Some tasks are sequential. Many aren't. But the default mode in a Claude Code session is linear: one thing, then the next. Planning a session upfront — here's what can run concurrently, here's what has to wait — and then actually executing that plan is harder than it should be.

Debussy is my attempt to fix all three. It's a meta-plugin: a plugin about using plugins better. The name is a small joke — Claude Debussy, the composer, was famous for structure beneath apparent improvisation. That felt right for a tool that adds formality to what is already a remarkably fluid experience.
It's early. The inception was last week. But the three problems it targets are real, and they compound each other. Worth building.
Claude Code is powerful out of the box. But once you start doing serious work, the gaps become visible — and fixable.
